subject: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR

messages.author: 82074a779b5b2fc0
messages.subject: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR
parts:
Dear all,

I am working with ordered data with 4 response categories. I have p(p+1)/2 = 45 information and 39 parameters to be estimated using WLSMV, 27 parameters to be estimated using MLR.

When I use WLSMV, I get a warning that the smallest eigenvalue is close to zero and that the model may not be identified (but all parameters including standard errors are estimated and in a sensible range). Using MLR, there are no warnings or errors. The parameter estimates are quite similar between both models, fit indices are fine (WLSMV has a slightly better fit), so I would come to the same conclusion independent of the model I choose.

I had the (maybe stupid?) idea of using using lavCov() to create a polychoric covariance matrix that I then can use as an input for ML estimation so I can at least partly account for the ordinal nature of the data. It works without problems, I obtain even better fit indices, similar parameter estimates, so again, I would come to the same conclusion.

So I was wondering what you would suggest as the best method? Can I ignore the warning, as estimation seems to be okay? Or is it sensible to use the polychoric covariance matrix, as this way the covariances that are used for estimation reflect the data better? Or would you go for an MLR estimation that allows for robust standard errors? I would be very happy for your ideas and suggestions!

Best Mirka

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR
parts: I had the (maybe stupid?) idea of using using lavCov() to create a polychoric covariance matrix that I then can use as an input for ML estimation

You can't trust the SEs or test statistics because they treat the polychorics as known observations rather than as estimates (with their own SEs).  Taking the uncertainty of the first-step estimates into account is what DWLS does.
I was wondering what you would suggest as the best method?
Depends how you define "best", and what your sample size is, and some other properties of the observed data, and some properties of the assumed latent responses if you use DWLS.
Can I ignore the warning, as estimation seems to be okay?
Probably, if there are no other signs of empirical underidentification.
Or is it sensible to use the polychoric covariance matrix, as this way the covariances that are used for estimation reflect the data better?

You cannot compare fit across those estimators because they are based on different (assumptions about the) data.  Under DWLS, your model only has to reproduce the estimated polychoric correlation matrix, not the actual observed response patterns.
Or would you go for an MLR estimation that allows for robust standard errors?

If the latent normal item response assumption holds, then this would underestimate factor loadings (to degrees that depend on the distribution of thresholds), but structural parameters tend to be pretty unbiased either way.  Whether the chi-squared has inflated errors additionally depends on sample size. 

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

Either choice is based on dubious assumptions, so it just depends on which ones you are more comfortable putting your faith in.

https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2020.589965

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
